text: Syslog, JSON, and CSV are the three formats you'll meet constantly in security automation -- firewall logs, EDR exports, threat-intel feeds, asset inventories. Each has a specific trap that quietly produces wrong results if you miss it. This lesson walks through all three with real Python, plus the one step that matters more than any of them: normalizing timestamps before correlating events across sources.

A syslog line packs a priority value, a timestamp, a hostname, a process and PID, and a free-text message into one string. Python doesn't ship a one-call syslog parser, since the message portion is vendor-specific text, but the structured prefix is regular enough to pull apart with a regex using named groups -- groupdict turns the match straight into a dictionary, instead of numbered groups nobody can read six months later.

Most cloud platforms and EDR agents now export events as JSON, often one object per line, a format called JSON Lines. Python's json module handles that with json dot loads in a simple loop. The real trap isn't syntax -- it's that one vendor's alert has severity as the string high, another has Severity as the number three, and a third nests it under properties dot level. You write a normalization function mapping every source into one consistent shape.

CSV shows up constantly too -- threat-intel feeds, CMDB asset lists, user exports from an identity provider. Python's csv dot DictReader handles quoted fields with embedded commas correctly, which manual comma-splitting gets wrong. Watch for three things: forgetting newline equals empty string in the open call; encoding surprises like cp1252 or a UTF-8 byte-order mark; and the fact that DictReader reads every value as a string, so a confidence of eighty-five is text, not a number, until converted.

Every format represents time differently -- syslog's no-year local-time string, a JSON log's ISO 8601 with a timezone offset, a CSV export's month-day-year format. Convert everything to a single timezone-aware UTC datetime object before correlating, and normalize field names the same way. Skipping this is one of the most common reasons a correlation script quietly produces wrong results -- events eight hours apart can look simultaneous simply because nobody normalized the clock.

You now have real Python patterns for all three formats: a regex with named groups for syslog, json dot loads plus normalization for JSON, and csv dot DictReader with its encoding and type gotchas for CSV. Next lesson, you'll apply these parsing skills to a widely used kind of security data: STIX objects and the TAXII protocol used to share threat intelligence between organizations.
